AGENTS.md — Orientation for GenomicBreaks

Source: AGENTS.md

This file orients contributors and AI coding sessions working on GenomicBreaks. For a detailed review of known engineering gaps, see CODE_REVIEW.md.

Status / urgency

There is no official public release of this package yet. Consequently, the engineering issues recorded in docs/code_review.md (license placeholder, missing CI, unpinned dependencies, etc.) are low urgency: fix them opportunistically, not as blockers. Do not let them stall feature work.

The detailed reusability/code-review notes are in CODE_REVIEW.md (repo root), not docs/code_review.md.

Commit Messages

When creating commits, include the line AI-generated: yes in the commit message body (not the subject line).

What this package is

An R package built on the Bioconductor ecosystem (but not part of it) for analysing pairwise whole-genome alignments where evolution has scrambled gene order. It loads alignments (GFF3 / MAF), coalesces colinear fragments, flags structural variants (inversions, translocations, double/twin inversions), computes synteny and nucleotide-distance metrics, and plots macrosynteny / Oxford / pair-of-chromosome figures.

Core data model

  • GBreaks is an S4 class wrapping GenomicRanges::GRanges (R/GenomicBreaks.R:22).
  • Main ranges = target genome coordinates.
  • query metadata column (a GRanges) = query genome coordinates.
  • Strand is carried on the target ranges; query ranges stay on the plus strand by convention.

Repository layout

Path Contents
R/ R source, one topic per file (see Collate: in DESCRIPTION).
src/ Rcpp C++ MAF reader (readMaf.cpp) + RcppExports.cpp; partly from LAST (GPLv3+).
data/ Lazy-loaded example datasets (example* objects).
data-raw/ Scripts that regenerate data/ and some inst/extdata/ files.
inst/extdata/ Small fixture files (GFF3, MAF, train) used by examples, and simulatedRearrangements.rds (200 simulated genome pairs stored as permutation vectors; see ?simulateRearrangements).

vignettes/ Long-form documentation (*.Rmd).
CODE_REVIEW.md Reusability/code-review study. Excluded from the build.

Build / check / document

Generated artefacts (man/, NAMESPACE, src/RcppExports.cpp) are produced by roxygen2/Rcpp — edit the source, then regenerate, never edit by hand.

R -e 'devtools::document()'      # regenerate man/ + NAMESPACE from roxygen
R -e 'devtools::load_all()'      # load for interactive work (compiles src/)
R CMD build .                    # build the source tarball
R CMD check GenomicBreaks_*.tar.gz   # full package check
R -e 'pkgdown::build_site()'     # rebuild the documentation site

Building the MAF reader requires a C++ toolchain (Rcpp). System prerequisites for a clean environment are listed in Singularity.def.

GitHub Actions currently only builds/deploys the pkgdown site (.github/workflows/pkgdown.yaml). It does not run R CMD check.

Conventions

  • roxygen2 in markdown mode (Config/roxygen2, DESCRIPTION Roxygen:). Document above each function; regenerate with devtools::document().
  • @family / @concept tags matter: the pkgdown reference index is grouped by them (_pkgdown.yml). Keep them on new exported functions.
  • S4 classes/methods via methods::setClass/setGeneric/setMethod.
  • Semantic versioning since 0.17.0; record every user-visible change in NEWS.md and bump the Version: in DESCRIPTION.
  • Keep roxygen @examples runnable on the bundled example data — they are currently a primary form of verification.

Structural-variant flags

Conventions

  • Flags are set on the first range of a pattern in target order (for example the left flank of an inversion triplet). The filter*, remove*, show* and flip* helpers find the other ranges by their offset from the flag. This has confused users and may change later; keep it for now.
  • Use precedeZW() and followZW() (internal, in R/dist2next.R) instead of GenomicRanges::precede() and follow() for adjacency tests: the latter report a zero-width range as adjacent to itself.
  • Look-ahead coding pattern (see flagDoubleInversions()):
    • qnext0 <- precedeZW(gb$query) - seq_along(gb$query) is the offset, in target order, of the range that range i immediately precedes on the query; qnextK <- c(tail(qnext0, -K), NA, ...) is the same for range i + K, and strandK is built the same way from strand(gb).
    • A pattern is an & chain of qnextK == value and strandK == "+" or "-" tests, piped to sapply(isTRUE) to turn NA into FALSE.
    • The expected qnext values of a pattern are precede(IPos(r)) - seq_along(r), where r is the query rank of each range in target order. The NA value (last range in query order) is not tested. Write this line as a comment above each pattern.
    • All ranges of a pattern must be on one target sequence; the query adjacencies already imply one query sequence.

Plan (agreed 2026-10-23)

  1. Fix the defects of the existing flagging functions with direct patches, one commit per issue.
  2. Then replace the hand-written patterns by a table generated by enumeration, matched by one function (compare allPossiblePairClasses in R/flagPairs.R). For k central ranges between two flanks that did not move relative to each other, enumerate all signed arrangements, keep those whose internal junctions are all breakpoints (coalesced input), and record for each its qnextK/strandK pattern, number of breakpoints b, minimal number of events d and breakpoint reuse rate 2d/b (Pevzner and Tesler 2003). Each arrangement then gets exactly one label.
  3. Parsimony: a translocation counts as one event, like an inversion. An arrangement explained by fewer events with a translocation must not be labelled as several inversions. Which moves count as one translocation (one range or a segment, inverted or not) is still to be decided.
  4. First enumeration (3 central ranges, inversions only, breadth-first search; lower case means minus strand, flanks on the plus strand): of the 48 arrangements, 25 have 4 breakpoints. b c A and C a b need two overlapping inversions (flagDoubleInversions()); a B c is two separate inversions and c B a two nested ones (both found by flagInversions()); the other 21 need three inversions (reuse rate 1.5), and are flagged only as translocations (10) or not at all (11). With 2 central ranges after coalescing: a b is a twin inversion, b A and B a need two inversions and B A three, and these three are flagged only as translocations. Triple inversions are to be revisited once translocations are included in the enumeration.
  5. Deferred: a function returning, for each inversion, both breakpoint regions on both genomes, computed from the coordinates of the triplet. leftInversionGaps() only returns the left one on the target genome.
  6. The show*, filter* and remove* helpers must work well and consistently for all structural variants (see the known issues below).

Known issues

Flags are relative to the target side, and fragile. A flag is a metadata column of the target ranges, and its meaning depends on the row order of the object. Any transformation of a GBreaks object (subsetting, sort(), c(), coalesce_contigs(), reverse(), swap()) can invalidate the flags or drop them, without warning. swap() drops the target metadata columns, flags included, and the remove* helpers drop them through coalesce_contigs(). Flags should be recomputed after a transformation.

Translocations (flagTranslocations(); tested against a brute-force implementation of its definition on the stored simulations):

  • The function finds transpositions (moves of one range, possibly inverted, on the same sequence or not) rather than translocations; do not rename it for now.
  • A move of range A is seen in two places of the target order, both flagged on the target ranges, without swap():
    • the payload region U A V: three consecutive target ranges, with U and V adjacent and colinear on the query. tra flag, on U; the payload is the next range.
    • the site X Y: two consecutive target ranges between which A is found on the query (X A Y). trs flag, on X. The pattern uses one indirect lookup: the payload is i + qnext0[i] (i + qprev0[i] on the minus strand), and the test is qnext0[i] != 1 & qnext0[i] + qnext0[i + qnext0[i]] == 1. When both are seen, they point to the same payload; either can be missing, for instance when A is alone on its sequence in one genome. Events can be built by pairing the two flags through their payload.
  • flagAll() only uses tra, on purpose for now: the X of a site can carry another flag, which would make its stopifnot() checks fail.
  • Before 0.25.0, the site was flagged with both = TRUE, by a tra flag on the query ranges computed through swap(); that flag was on Y for minus-strand sites, and on the wrong row when target ranges were duplicated.
  • tol limits the distances between the ranges that must be adjacent: U A V on the target and U V on the query for payload regions, X Y on the target and X A Y on the query for sites.
  • The show*, filter* and remove* helpers use both flags; the moved ranges are computed by the internal translocationPayloads().

Strandless ranges (strand *). They come from (1) objects that are unoriented as a whole, for instance made from reciprocal best hits, and (2) mapped regions (bridgeRegions()), which materialise the unaligned region between two colinear alignments, possibly with a width of zero on one or both genomes (in Plessy et al. 2024, some are new short introns). Rule: process when possible, ignore when needed, error when unavoidable. The behaviour of all functions on such ranges is experimental (stated in NEWS.md and in an “Unstranded ranges (experimental)” section of the help pages), so that it can change without a breaking change. State (decided 2026-10-24):

  • Inversions (simple, double, twin) are never flagged when a range of the pattern is unstranded.
  • Colinearity treats * as compatible with both strands, as GenomicRanges does, and adjacency in either direction counts for * pairs. Works on unoriented objects and on mapped regions of non-zero width.
  • coalesce_contigs() merges unoriented objects. In mixed objects, it coalesces the oriented ranges and absorbs the mapped regions that they contain on both genomes; other mapped regions are returned unchanged.
  • flagTranslocations() tests * ranges in both directions. Extra ranges are then flagged as moved (target X Y U A V, query X A Y U V: Y and U too, because moving A over Y U is also moving Y U over A); this was accepted and documented. A stricter criterion for unoriented data could require the moved range not to be adjacent to the flanks on the other genome. flagAll() gives colinearity precedence over Tra on * ranges, where the two can coincide.
  • flagPairs(): pairs that involve * are Col, Scr, or NA when undetermined; the factor levels must not change.
  • permutationVector() stops with an error on * ranges, which also stops inversionDistance() and breakpointGraphProperties().
  • Zero-width ranges: precede() reports a zero-width range as preceding itself (and follow() as following itself), and breaks ties by index. The adjacency tests use precedeZW() and followZW(), which place zero-width ranges between the bases that surround them (done; tested by adding zero-width bridges to simulations, which must not change the flags of the alignments).

Helpers (show*, filter*, remove*, flip*):

  • Double inversions: there is no showDoubleInversions().
  • Twin inversions: there are no show*, filter* or remove* functions.
  • filterColinearRegions() has no detect argument.
  • The detect argument is documented as “reuse the flag or fail if it is absent”, but the helpers return an empty object instead of failing; for the remove* functions, an empty object is especially misleading.
  • Only show* and filter* have a rename argument.
  • removeDoubleInversions() returns early for objects of fewer than 3 ranges, instead of 5.

Testing (please help here)

Verification today rests heavily on vignettes + man-page examples.

Unit tests are in tests/testthat/ (testthat, edition 3); run them with R -e 'devtools::test()'. Do not remove the existing vignette/@examples coverage; add tests incrementally.

For structural variants, simulateRearrangements() and permutationVectorToGBreaks() build test objects from known events or signed permutations, and the simulations in inst/extdata/simulatedRearrangements.rds can be compared with an independent, brute-force implementation of a flag’s definition.

Use the lazy-loaded example* objects in the tests as much as possible. Build an object by hand only when no example fits, and in that case propose a new example (in data-raw/StructuralVariants.R) when it would also fill a missing role in the man-page examples. Candidates from the hand-built objects of the current tests:

  • a transposition along one sequence, seen at both its payload region and its site (target X Y U A V, query X A Y U V; currently permutationVectorToGBreaks(c(1, 3, 4, 2, 5)));
  • colinear alignments with their mapped regions, including zero-width ones and one of width zero on the query only (a new intron in the target);
  • an unoriented object (all ranges on the * strand), as made from reciprocal best hits;
  • an inversion triplet whose query adjacency is interrupted by range 1 (regression test for flagInversions() and flagPairs()).

Lift existing @examples into expect_* assertions. High-value candidates include the colinearity/coalescing functions and the nucleotide-distance functions (some distance functions are explicitly flagged as not-yet-proofread in NEWS.md).
